docs.shadowCaster.component: `ShadowCaster` declares that a shadow FALLS under this element — and which contour falls:
`footprint` is the bare box a piece stands on, `silhouette` (the default) the contour as drawn,
corners and all. The shadow itself is NOT a node: it is a layer the scene plan draws in one
pass, under everything at rest, in the `shadow` theme token thinned by a stock opacity.
```ts
import { node, Bounded, Surfaced, Transformable, ShadowCaster, Lit } from "game-kit"
const desk = node("desk", Container({ layout: "free" }), Lit())   // the one lamp
const card = node("card",
Bounded({ bounds: rect(1, 1.4) }),
Surfaced({ surface: "queen" }),
Transformable({ at: { x: 0, y: 0 }, z: 1 }),
ShadowCaster())                                                   // silhouette falls
## Height is the source, the shadow its consequence
There is no shadow-length knob. The fall's direction is the root lamp's (`Lit`), and its reach
grows with the resolved `z` — lift a piece and its shadow stretches, drop it and a hair of
shadow remains, or nothing would say the piece is not painted on the desk. Zoom never changes
the shadow-to-size ratio: the world scales whole.
## A resting stack casts once
Cast-ness is derived, never toggled: the nearest casting owner speaks for its whole subtree, so
a pile with the atom lays ONE shadow and the fifty-two cards inside lay none. Detach a card and
it starts casting the moment it stands alone — reparenting IS the switch. The fall also ignores
every angle: a turned piece turns its silhouette, never the direction of its shadow.
docs.shadowCaster.cast: A rounded card and a star token under one lamp. `from` picks the contour that falls — on the
card, `silhouette` keeps the rounded corners and `footprint` squares them off; on the star the
two agree, because its box IS its drawn shape. `z` lifts both pieces, and the fall stretches
with the height; `lampAngle` walks the light around the desk and every shadow answers together.
docs.shadowCaster.stack: A pile that casts once. The pile carries the atom, so the three cards resting inside lay no
shadows of their own — one stack, one shadow. The loose card beside it stands alone and casts
alone. Nothing here is toggled: moving a card out of the pile is exactly what starts its shadow.
